passage:
Supervisor's note, soil testing lab, Guwahati. Bhupen, 12 July.
Sabina had to email the tea estate that their samples were contaminated and needed re-testing, which meant a two-week delay. The email was maybe six lines. On Monday she told me she'd send it "after lunch". On Tuesday it was "first thing tomorrow". On Wednesday I saw her open the draft, stare at it, then go and rinse glassware that was already clean. When I asked, she said quietly, "They'll be furious, and they'll ask why we didn't catch it." I sat with her and we read the draft aloud once. It was fine. She pressed send at 3:10 and let out a long breath. The estate manager replied within the hour: "Thanks for telling us. Please go ahead."

qa.q: What was wrong with the tea estate's samples?
qa.a: The samples were contaminated and needed re-testing.

qa.q: Why did Sabina rinse glassware that was already clean?
qa.a: She dreaded the estate's anger and questions 😰, so a harmless chore let her escape the draft; a six-line email was carrying a very large feeling.

qa.q: What choice did Bhupen make on Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Bhupen sat with Sabina and read the draft aloud once; hearing that it was fine shrank the fear enough for her to press send.

qa.q: How might the estate manager have felt if the email had come a week later?
qa.a: The manager would probably have been more frustrated, losing time to plan around the delay; the quick, calm reply suggests early honesty was what they needed.

grounding: An adult keeps postponing a short email about a delay because she dreads the reaction, until her supervisor helps her send it.

passage:
Sunday, 11 p.m.
Day six of not emailing Mrs D'Souza. It's a two-line email. "Dear Ma'am, I won't be renewing my contract at the school after June. Thank you for everything." That's IT. I've written it, deleted it, rewritten it. Every time the cursor goes near Send, my chest squeezes and I suddenly need to clean the fridge. 😰
She hired me when nobody else would. I keep picturing her face going cold.
Afreen called tonight: "Is the email out?" Me: "Tomorrow." Afreen: "You said that on Tuesday." She's right.
The fridge is spotless. The email is still in drafts. Somehow two lines weigh more than the whole fridge.
Plan: send it at 8 a.m., before tea, before thinking.
- Zubin

qa.q: How many days has Zubin gone without emailing Mrs D'Souza?
qa.a: It is day six of not emailing Mrs D'Souza.

qa.q: What is Zubin afraid of when the cursor goes near Send?
qa.a: Zubin keeps picturing Mrs D'Souza's face going cold and feeling ungrateful to someone who took a chance, so the fear of that reaction makes two lines feel enormous.

qa.q: What plan does Zubin make, and why might it work?
qa.a: Sending it at 8 a.m., before tea and before thinking; a fixed, early moment gives the dread less time to build up.

qa.q: What might Afreen be feeling during the call?
qa.a: Afreen seems to have noticed the pattern and cares enough to point it out gently, perhaps worried that each delay is making Zubin more anxious, not less.

grounding: An adult postpones a two-line resignation email for days because of dread about the response, while cleaning instead.

passage: Lakshmi, you asked how I finally finished that translation job after ghosting it for two weeks. Honestly? I stopped shouting at myself. For days I'd open the file, think, you useless, lazy person, the client trusted you, and close it again. The worse I felt, the more I stayed away. Then one night my old hostel-mate said on the phone, "Would you talk to me like that?" No. Never. So the next morning I said out loud, like an idiot in my kitchen, "Okay, Bidisha, you got behind. It happens. Five minutes, that's all." I set a timer. Five minutes became forty. Next day, same deal. I'm still behind sometimes, still guilty sometimes. But now I keep coming back.

qa.q: What did Bidisha say out loud in the kitchen?
qa.a: 'Okay, Bidisha, you got behind. It happens. Five minutes, that's all.'

qa.q: Why did the harsh self-talk make Bidisha stay away from the file even more?
qa.a: Every time the file opened, the insults piled guilt onto it, so the work itself began to feel like a punishment worth escaping.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what made the fresh start work?
qa.a: The hostel-mate's question, 'Would you talk to me like that?'; speaking kindly and promising only five minutes made starting feel safe, and five minutes grew to forty.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi take from hearing this?
qa.a: Lakshmi might feel allowed to be gentler about delays of their own, seeing that Bidisha still feels guilty at times yet keeps returning to the work.

grounding: An adult stops berating themselves over a delayed job, forgives the delay and commits to five minutes, which leads back to the work.

passage: I'm Vikas, and I share a desk partition with Sunaina at the architecture firm. For most of October the heritage-building report sat untouched on her screen. I'd hear her mutter, "What is wrong with you," and then she'd switch to emails, or go for a third chai. She looked more miserable every day. Last Monday something was different. She stuck a note on her monitor: "Late isn't bad. Five minutes." She set a phone timer, and when it rang she didn't stop; she was still typing an hour later. I asked if she'd found some secret. She shrugged. "I stopped calling myself names. It's easier to come back when nobody's yelling at me, even me." I don't know everything that changed, but the report went out on Friday.

qa.q: What did the note on Sunaina's monitor say?
qa.a: 'Late isn't bad. Five minutes.'

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling during October, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She seemed guilty and stuck; muttering 'What is wrong with you' and escaping into emails or chai show self-blame pushing her away from the report.

qa.q: Which change helped Sunaina return to the report?
qa.a: Dropping the self-insults and committing to a five-minute timer; with less guilt attached, starting was bearable and she kept going for an hour.

qa.q: How might sitting beside Sunaina have felt different for Vikas after Monday?
qa.a: Vikas was likely relieved and a little curious, hearing typing instead of muttering, and glad to see a colleague looking less miserable.

grounding: A colleague sees an adult stop berating herself over a delayed report and commit to five minutes, after which she keeps working.

passage: At nine every night in their Mumbai flat, the pressure cooker next door gave its last whistle, and Leela, eight, put down her crayons without being asked. Brush teeth at the small basin, change into the blue pyjamas, climb into bed, wait for her mother, Seema, to open the storybook with the torn cover. One chapter, lights off. Leela didn't think about any of it anymore. The steps just rolled one into the next. One Saturday her cousin stayed over and wanted to watch TV late. Leela yawned, walked to the basin, and was halfway through brushing before she even noticed. "You're like a clock," her cousin laughed. Leela shrugged, spitting out toothpaste. "I just go."

qa.q: What sound came at nine every night?
qa.a: The pressure cooker next door gave its last whistle.

qa.q: What does 'I just go' suggest about how bedtime feels to Leela?
qa.a: Leela feels calm and at ease at bedtime; the steps are automatic rather than choices, so bedtime happens without a struggle.

qa.q: What choice could Seema make on nights when the routine is disturbed, like a cousin's visit?
qa.a: Keep the same order of steps, brushing, pyjamas and one chapter, even if the time shifts, so the familiar chain still carries Leela to sleep.

qa.q: How might the cousin see Leela's bedtime?
qa.a: The cousin, who wanted to stay up, might find it funny or puzzling that Leela leaves the TV with nobody telling her, as if a clock had ticked.

grounding: A child whose bedtime steps happen at the same time every night finds herself moving through them automatically.

passage:
"Sharmila, it's half past eight."
"I know, Paati, I'm going." Sharmila was already at the sink with her toothbrush.
Minakshi Paati laughed. "In summer you fought me every single night."
"That was before." Sharmila spat and rinsed. "Now my feet just walk here."
"And then?"
"Then nightie, then your story, then sleep. Same as always."
"Tonight Appa's calling from Muscat at nine. Maybe you'll stay up for him?"
Sharmila frowned. "Can he call at ten to nine? My eyes close after the story."
"Your eyes know the time better than the clock."
"Paati, today's story is the crow and the pot. You promised."
"Brushed?"
"Brushed."
"Then come."

qa.q: Which story did Paati promise for tonight?
qa.a: The crow and the pot.

qa.q: What does 'Now my feet just walk here' show about how Sharmila feels about bedtime?
qa.a: Sharmila feels settled and calm about bedtime now; it is no longer a fight or a decision, and the steps come by themselves.

qa.q: What choice does Sharmila make about Appa's call, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: She asks if Appa can call at ten to nine, keeping her routine instead of staying up, because she knows her eyes close after the story.

qa.q: What is bedtime like for Minakshi Paati now compared with the summer?
qa.a: Minakshi Paati no longer has to battle Sharmila every night, so the evening feels lighter and she can simply enjoy telling the story 😊

grounding: A child whose bedtime order never changes walks through brushing, story and sleep without being pushed.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage: I'm Madhav. Shankar and I ride the same school van, and I've started noticing something. The van stops at the railway crossing for maybe two minutes. Before the gate is even down, Shankar's phone is out. At the petrol pump, phone. When the driver waits for the twins near the park, phone. He doesn't message anyone. He just flicks: a funny clip, a cricket score, a meme he doesn't even laugh at. Yesterday I asked, "What are you looking for?" He looked at the phone as if he'd found it in his hand by surprise. "Nothing, I guess." Then the van moved and he kept scrolling. I can't see inside his head, but it looked less like a choice and more like a reflex.

qa.q: Where does the van stop for about two minutes?
qa.a: At the railway crossing.

qa.q: Why might Shankar reach for the phone at every stop without meaning to?
qa.a: Each pause feels empty and a bit dull, and a quick new clip gives a small lift; repeated often enough, his hand now moves before he decides.

qa.q: What could Shankar try at the next van stop, and why?
qa.a: Keep the phone zipped in his bag during stops and look out or chat with Madhav instead; a harder-to-reach phone breaks the automatic pause-to-scroll link.

qa.q: How does the habit look from Madhav's seat?
qa.a: To Madhav it looks like a reflex rather than a choice, and it may feel a little lonely to sit beside someone whose attention keeps slipping to a screen.

grounding: A classmate notices a teenager pull out the phone at every pause and scroll without meaning to.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage:
Monday: Waiting for the microwave to beep, Aditi, sixteen, found her phone already in her hand. Same between two maths sums, same while her friend Ishita tied her shoelaces before PT. Aditi hadn't decided anything; her thumb was just moving.
Thursday: Ishita dared her to move a coin from her left pocket to her right every time she picked up the phone for no reason. By lunch Aditi had moved it twenty-three times. "Every single boring second," she said, stunned. "I grab it just to see something new."
The next Tuesday: She kept a small puzzle book in her blazer pocket. At the microwave, her hand still twitched toward the pocket, but she filled in three squares instead.

qa.q: How many times had Aditi moved the coin by lunch on Thursday?
qa.a: By lunch Aditi had moved it twenty-three times.

qa.q: What did Aditi realise about why she grabs the phone?
qa.a: She saw that boredom sets it off: in every dull second her hand reaches for something new, not because she has chosen to.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Aditi change after it?
qa.a: Counting the grabs on Thursday made the loop visible; she then kept a puzzle book in her pocket, giving her hand a different action at the same cue.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel about the dare turning into a real change?
qa.a: Ishita may be pleased and a little proud that a playful dare helped a friend see the habit, and curious whether the puzzle book will last.

grounding: A teenager discovers she picks up the phone at every bored moment without deciding to, and replaces the action.

passage:
At 4:20, Francis texted his son from the office.
Dad: home?
Samir: yeah
Dad: on the sofa?
Samir: ...how do u know
Dad: 😄 I watched last week. bag drops, sofa, phone. every day. then suddenly it's 7
Samir: ok and? I'm tired after school
Dad: not a lecture. I'd grab the phone too if I sat there
Dad: new idea. charger's moved to the dining table. snack's on the balcony chair
Samir: you moved the SOFA charger??
Dad: yes. eat outside, then homework at the dining table. phone charges there till you're done
Samir: this is so sneaky
Dad: 🙂 try it this week. if it's awful we'll change it
Samir: fine. but the sofa's mine on Sunday
Dad: deal 👍

qa.q: Where did Dad move the charger?
qa.a: The charger's moved to the dining table.

qa.q: What does Francis's 'not a lecture' suggest about his thinking?
qa.a: He has realised that nagging doesn't help and that the sofa itself sets off the habit, so he wants Samir to feel understood rather than blamed.

qa.q: What choice did Francis make instead of nagging, and why could it work?
qa.a: He changed the setting: charger at the dining table, snack on the balcony; without the sofa-and-charger cue, the phone is no longer the first thing Samir reaches for.

qa.q: How might Samir feel about the change?
qa.a: Samir sounds annoyed at first ('so sneaky') but also relieved not to be scolded, and bargaining for Sunday shows he is willing to try it.

grounding: A parent notices the phone habit starts when his son sits on the sofa after school, and changes the setting instead of nagging.

passage: In their house at the edge of Hosapete, the charpai on the verandah was where everything happened. Manjula, fifteen, came home from school, dropped onto it, and within a minute the family phone was in her hands. Devika watched this for a week from the kitchen door while grinding masala. She had said "Enough now" so many times that Manjula no longer heard it. So on Saturday Devika tried something else. She moved the charpai to the back yard, put the plug board on the kitchen wall, and set a small table on the verandah with a lamp and Manjula's books. On Monday Manjula came home, looked for the charpai, frowned, and sat at the table. The phone stayed charging in the kitchen till she finished her science.

qa.q: Where did Devika put the plug board?
qa.a: On the kitchen wall.

qa.q: Why had Devika stopped saying 'Enough now'?
qa.a: Devika felt frustrated that Manjula no longer heard it, so repeating it seemed pointless and she wanted something that would actually change the afternoons.

qa.q: What did Devika change, and why did it work better than nagging?
qa.a: She moved the charpai, the plug board and the books, so the old spot that started the habit was gone; without that cue, the phone wasn't the first thing Manjula reached for.

qa.q: What might Monday afternoon have felt like for Manjula?
qa.a: A little confusing and annoying at first, with her usual spot gone, but with no scolding involved, sitting down at the table was easy to accept.

grounding: A mother sees her teenager's phone habit start on the verandah charpai and rearranges the space instead of nagging.

passage: Rehana, I saw you open that packet of chakli the moment your professor's email arrived. Sit, let me tell you about me at twenty, in the hostel in Bhubaneswar. I'm Jyoti, remember, not always this calm. Every time a test result was due, my stomach twisted. My hand went straight to the tin of murukku from home. Ten minutes of crunching and I felt calm, and soon I felt calm only with the tin. By the end of the year I was reaching for it before I'd even read the notice. One evening my roommate asked, "What happens right before you open the tin?" I actually thought about it. Worry. Then tin. Then relief. Once I saw it in three pieces, I could change the middle one. I started walking to the water cooler and back instead. Not magic. But I knew where to cut.

qa.q: What did young Jyoti reach for when a test result was due?
qa.a: The tin of murukku from home.

qa.q: Why did the murukku tin feel so necessary to young Jyoti?
qa.a: Worry twisted Jyoti's stomach, and ten minutes of crunching brought quick calm, so each time the tin seemed like the obvious answer to the feeling.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Jyoti, and what changed after it?
qa.a: The roommate's question about what comes right before the tin; seeing worry, tin and relief as three parts let Jyoti swap the middle for a walk to the water cooler.

qa.q: What might Rehana start to notice about the chakli after hearing this?
qa.a: Rehana might see that the professor's email set off the reach for the packet, and begin noticing the worry that comes first.

grounding: An elder recalls how, as a stressed student, seeing the snacking as worry, snack and relief showed which step to change.

passage: It was Harish's second-year exam week, the hostel mess had shut early for a festival, and the Wi-Fi kept dropping. Every time he opened the thermodynamics notes and hit a problem he couldn't solve, his chest tightened and he grabbed his phone. With the Wi-Fi down, he couldn't scroll. So he grabbed a packet of banana chips instead, then another. Ojas, his roommate, looked up from the other bed. "You do that every time a problem gets hard, you know. Stuck, then snack, then five minutes of feeling okay." Harish stared at the empty packets. He hadn't noticed the stuck part at all. That night he wrote on a sticky note: When stuck, stand up, drink water, try one more line. It didn't fix everything, but now he could see the loop.

qa.q: Why couldn't Harish scroll that week?
qa.a: The Wi-Fi kept dropping.

qa.q: Why did Harish keep reaching for snacks when a problem got hard?
qa.a: Being stuck tightened his chest, and a snack brought five minutes of feeling okay; that brief relief made reaching again feel natural.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Harish plan after it?
qa.a: Ojas naming the sequence, stuck, snack, feeling okay; Harish then wrote a new response for the same trigger: stand up, drink water, try one more line.

qa.q: How might Ojas feel after pointing out the loop?
qa.a: Ojas may have felt unsure about speaking up but glad it helped, since Harish took it as useful rather than as criticism.

grounding: A stressed student reaches for snacks or scrolling for brief relief, and naming the loop's parts shows him where to change it.

passage:
Dear Jyoti,
Remember how I said I'd start running in January and you bet me a samosa I'd quit by the 10th? The old me would have lost. Every morning I had to hunt for shoes, socks and a clean T-shirt, and by then my blanket had won the argument.
So here's what changed. Every night the shoes go right beside my bed, socks stuffed inside, T-shirt folded on top. And my goal is only ten minutes, once round the hostel block. Ten! Some days I feel silly, it's so small. But on the cold mornings those ten minutes are the only reason I get out at all, and most days I end up doing twenty.
It's week five. I owe you nothing. 😊
Love,
Ankita

qa.q: Where does Ankita put the running shoes each night?
qa.a: Right beside the bed, socks stuffed inside, T-shirt folded on top.

qa.q: Why does Ankita sometimes feel silly about the ten-minute goal?
qa.a: It seems almost too small to count, yet Ankita also knows that on cold mornings that small target is what makes getting out possible.

qa.q: Which change mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Laying everything by the bed and keeping the target to ten minutes; there is nothing to hunt for and nothing big to dread, so the start beats the blanket.

qa.q: What might Jyoti think on reading 'I owe you nothing'?
qa.a: Jyoti will probably laugh at losing the bet and be glad, maybe impressed, that the running has lasted into week five.

grounding: A student lays out running shoes by the bed and sets a ten-minute target, and the new habit survives its first weeks.

passage: Harish, you asked how I kept running this time when I quit three times last year? Okay. I'm Parul, and I am not a morning person. Last year I'd plan a proper five-kilometre run, and by day four I'd wake up, think five kilometres, and roll over. This time I did two things. First, I sleep in my track pants, and my shoes wait beside the bed with the laces already loose, so I can step straight in. Second, the promise is just ten minutes: out to the bus stand and back. Most days that's all I do. Some days I keep going. It's been two months now, and the shoes have left a faint mark on the floor tile. That mark makes me weirdly proud.

qa.q: What is Parul's ten-minute route?
qa.a: Out to the bus stand and back.

qa.q: Why did Parul roll over by day four last year?
qa.a: Picturing a full five kilometres made getting up feel huge, so staying in bed seemed like the reasonable choice in that sleepy moment.

qa.q: What two choices helped Parul's habit survive this time?
qa.a: Sleeping in track pants with loose-laced shoes by the bed, and promising only ten minutes; the start became nearly effortless and too small to argue with.

qa.q: What might Harish take from Parul's story?
qa.a: Harish might see that a new habit needs an easy start more than a big one, and try shrinking a goal of Harish's own.

grounding: A student sleeps in track pants beside ready shoes and promises only ten minutes, so the running habit lasts.

passage:
Staff wellbeing session notes, 18 June. Ishita, counsellor.
Aditi, a call-centre team lead, came in about what she called "stress scrolling". After a hard customer call she reaches for her phone and scrolls for fifteen or twenty minutes. She has deleted the apps twice and reinstalled them within days. We talked about what the scrolling gives her: a break, a few minutes where nobody needs anything from her. So we kept the cue, the end of a hard call, and swapped the action: stand up, walk to the stairwell window and back, or three slow breaths if she can't leave the desk. She tracks it on a card, tick or cross. Today she showed me two weeks of cards, mostly ticks. "I still want the phone sometimes," she said. "But I don't need it the same way."

qa.q: How many times had Aditi deleted the apps?
qa.a: She has deleted the apps twice.

qa.q: Why does the scrolling feel so needed to Aditi after a hard call?
qa.a: Aditi feels stressed and drained after a hard call, and scrolling gives her a short break where nobody needs anything from her; without something else meeting that need, she keeps pulling the apps back.

qa.q: What choice did Ishita and Aditi make, and why did it work better than deleting?
qa.a: They kept the same cue, the end of a hard call, and swapped the action for a stairwell walk or three breaths, so Aditi still gets her break, and the card shows how it goes.

qa.q: How might Aditi's team experience the change?
qa.a: The team may find her back sooner and more present after tough calls, since a short walk gives her the pause without pulling her into a screen.

grounding: An adult keeps the cue for stress scrolling but swaps in a walk or breathing and tracks it, so the need for a break is still met.

passage:
Wed, 9:40 p.m.
Week three of the swap. Recap for future me: every evening after the hospital shift I'd sit on the steps outside the flat and scroll for an hour. Felt like rest. Wasn't. Tried just not scrolling. Lasted two evenings.
Sudha's idea: keep the steps, keep the sitting down. Swap the phone for one loop around the park, ten minutes, and mark it on the calendar.
Tonight: sat on the steps, hand went to my pocket by itself. Took the phone out, left it on the shoe rack inside, walked the loop. The neem trees smelled of rain. Came back actually feeling switched off.
Calendar: 14 green ticks, 4 red crosses. Not perfect. Better.
- Mohit

qa.q: How many green ticks were on the calendar?
qa.a: 14 green ticks, 4 red crosses.

qa.q: Why did scrolling on the steps feel like rest to Mohit?
qa.a: Mohit was tired after the hospital shift and needed to switch off; scrolling seemed restful, even though it never truly refreshed.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Sudha's idea, and why did it work where quitting failed?
qa.a: Keeping the steps and the sitting down but swapping the phone for a ten-minute park loop; the need to unwind was still met, so the change lasted.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel seeing the calendar?
qa.a: Sudha would probably be glad the idea helped and not bothered by the red crosses, since the ticks show real progress 😊

grounding: An adult keeps the after-shift cue of sitting on the steps but replaces scrolling with a short walk and tracks it.

subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
passage:
Friday: Ten minutes after lunch, Raghav, five, flopped on the floor. "Hemant Chacha, I'm bored! Give me the phone." Chacha said no. Raghav wailed and kicked a cushion.
Sunday: "Bored!" again. This time Chacha put down old newspapers, a glue stick and some bottle caps, and went back to his tea. Raghav sulked. Then he tore a strip of paper. Then another.
Wednesday: After lunch Raghav said, "I'm bored," and went to the newspapers by himself. By teatime a paper snake with bottle-cap eyes stretched across the floor. "His name is Tuktuk," Raghav said proudly.

qa.q: What did Raghav make by teatime on Wednesday?
qa.a: A paper snake with bottle-cap eyes.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when he wailed and kicked the cushion on Friday?
qa.a: He felt restless and frustrated; being bored was uncomfortable, and he wanted the phone to make that feeling go away fast.

qa.q: Which choice by Hemant Chacha made the difference?
qa.a: On Sunday he gave simple materials and time, then left Raghav alone; the sulky boredom turned into tearing, gluing and a snake called Tuktuk.

qa.q: What might Hemant Chacha feel seeing Tuktuk across the floor?
qa.a: Probably proud and amused 😊, glad he held back the phone long enough for Raghav's own ideas to show up.

subtype: Restless and asking what to do [Actor]
passage: Rain had drummed on the tin roof in Darjeeling for three days, the power was out, and the tablet was dead. Ira, five, pressed her nose to the window. "Ama, I'm bored. There's NOTHING." Pema was stirring thukpa by candlelight. She handed Ira an empty shoebox, some wool and a few clothes pegs. "Here. I'm busy for a bit." Ira pushed the box away and moaned on the rug. Then she picked up a peg and made it walk. Soon the pegs had wool hair, the shoebox was their house, and one peg was a grandmother scolding the others. When Pema looked over, Ira was whispering all the voices.

qa.q: What did Pema hand to Ira?
qa.a: An empty shoebox, some wool and a few clothes pegs.

qa.q: Why did Ira push the box away and moan at first?
qa.a: She felt bored and shut in and wanted the tablet; the plain box didn't look like fun yet, so being bored still felt awful.

qa.q: What choice by Pema helped Ira's boredom turn into play?
qa.a: Handing over simple things and then staying busy instead of entertaining her; with time and no screen, Ira invented a whole peg family.

qa.q: What might Pema feel hearing Ira whisper all the voices?
qa.a: Pema might feel relieved and quietly delighted that, even in a power cut, Ira found her own game.

grounding: A young child stuck indoors complains of boredom and wants a screen, then plays imaginatively with simple materials and time.

subtype: Bored by a class that is too easy or too hard [Actor]
passage: I used to think I was just lazy at maths. I'm Yash. In Class 9 I moved from a small school in Jalgaon to a big one in Pune, and on my first day the teacher was already on quadratic equations. We'd never even done factorisation properly back home. So I sat by the window and drew aeroplanes on the back page. The teacher's voice turned into noise. My report card said "inattentive". It was Aadhya, the girl next to me, who asked one day, "Are you bored, or are you lost?" I didn't know there was a difference. I was lost. Once I started staying back on Thursdays for the catch-up class, the aeroplanes mostly stopped. Turns out I could pay attention. I just had nothing to hold on to.

qa.q: What did Yash draw on the back page?
qa.a: Yash drew aeroplanes on the back page.

qa.q: Why did the teacher's voice turn into noise for Yash?
qa.a: The lesson was far beyond what Yash had learned in Jalgaon, so nothing connected; drifting off felt like the only way to sit through it.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what change followed?
qa.a: Aadhya's question, 'Are you bored, or are you lost?'; realising it was being lost led Yash to the Thursday catch-up class, and the doodling mostly stopped.

qa.q: How might the maths teacher read Yash differently after the catch-up classes?
qa.a: The teacher might see that 'inattentive' was really a gap in basics, not a lack of effort, and check for such gaps when new students join.

grounding: A teenager doodles and stares out of the window because the lesson is far beyond what they know, which looks like laziness but is a mismatch.

subtype: Bored by a class that is too easy or too hard [Actor]
passage:
Science teacher's note, Class 8B. Reena, 5 September.
For three weeks Joseph has spent my lessons on electricity drawing tiny comic strips in the margin and staring at the playground. I wrote "needs to focus" in his diary. Then on Tuesday I asked him a question to catch him out, and he explained series and parallel circuits more clearly than I had. At break he admitted he'd read the whole chapter in the summer and built a circuit with his uncle. "I'm not trying to be rude, Ma'am. I just already know it." I've crossed out my diary note. From next week he'll get an extension sheet: design the wiring for a model house. I'll watch whether the comic strips stop.

qa.q: What did Joseph draw in the margin?
qa.a: Tiny comic strips.

qa.q: How did Joseph seem to feel about the lessons, and what shows it?
qa.a: He seemed bored and a little uneasy about looking rude; the comics and the staring show his attention drifting because the work was far below him.

qa.q: What choice did Reena make after Tuesday, and why does it fit?
qa.a: She crossed out 'needs to focus' and planned an extension sheet on wiring a model house, matching the work to what Joseph already knows.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt when Joseph explained circuits more clearly than the lesson had?
qa.a: Reena was probably surprised and a little embarrassed about the 'needs to focus' note, which is why Reena crossed it out and planned an extension sheet.

grounding: A teacher realises a teenager's doodling comes from a lesson far below his level, not laziness, and adjusts the work.
